problem: Given that $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2$ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-3$ at the point where $\theta =\pi ,$ find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$
worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-3$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =(-3)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =(-3)\cdot (-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
